sections.label: Criminal law based on case law
sections.summary: Contempt's diverse forms make it not fully understood, and it is Singapore's only case-law-based criminal law, which is unsatisfactory as criminal laws must be in statute.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: They do not understand it fully because of its diverse forms.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It is the only criminal law in Singapore that is based on case law.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: That is not satisfactory because criminal laws must be set out in statute.

sections.label: Unlimited contempt punishment
sections.summary: The punishment for contempt is unlimited, unlike other criminal laws.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The punishment for contempt is unlimited, unlike other criminal laws.

sections.label: Clauses 3 and 4 conduct
sections.summary: Clauses 3 and 4 set out conduct amounting to contempt: disobeying Court orders, interfering with Court proceedings, sub judice contempt, and scandalising the Court.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The heart of the Bill is found in clauses 3 and 4.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: These clauses set out conduct which amounts to contempt: disobeying Court orders, interfering with Court proceedings, sub judice contempt; and scandalising the Court.

sections.label: Raised punishment for lower Courts
sections.summary: Because most disputes are heard and resolved in the lower Courts, the maximum punishment for the lower Courts was raised to signal such conduct will not be tolerated.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Most disputes are heard and resolved in the lower Courts.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We have, therefore, raised the maximum punishment vis-a-vis the lower Courts, to send a clear signal that such conduct will not be tolerated.

sections.label: State Courts criminal charges
sections.summary: Every year, approximately 60,000 criminal charges are dealt with by the State Courts.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Every year, approximately 60,000 criminal charges are dealt with by the State Courts.

sections.label: Clause reflects existing common law
sections.summary: The clause reflects the existing common law and does not change it, and one suggestion is to add "seriously" before "prejudice" in clause 3(1)(b).

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: As I do so, I should make clear that the clause reflects the existing common law; it does not change the common law.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: One suggestion is to add the word "seriously" before "prejudice" in clause 3(1)(b) so that the contempt is actionable only if it "seriously prejudices" Court proceedings.

sections.label: Real risk of prejudicing cases
sections.summary: The speaker says changing the law to allow prejudicing ongoing cases requires cogent reasons, and rejects qualifying clause 3(1)(b) with a public discussion defence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Or has a serious risk – real risk – I should use the words in the Bill – real risk of prejudicing a specific case.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This legal position has worked well for us all these years.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: If you want to change the law, if you want the right to prejudice ongoing cases, you have to put out cogent reasons why; why your right to speak and prejudice an ongoing trial should override someone else's right to a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It is for the same reason I cannot agree to any suggestion that clause 3(1)(b) be qualified by some general provision that provides for discussion by the public as a defence.

sections.label: Protecting rights of fair trial
sections.summary: The speaker says they protect all Singaporeans and that it would be shocking to put a commenter's rights above a person facing trial for a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We are here to protect all Singaporeans, including those voices which are not heard – the majority.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It will be quite shocking for us to say that the rights of someone who wishes to comment should be put above the rights of the person who is facing a trial, for a fair trial.

sections.label: Public mood pressures trial
sections.summary: When a public mood is created, everyone in the trial, including the judge, will be under pressure.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: When a public mood is created, everyone in the trial will be under pressure, including the judge.

sections.label: Charging not by public opinion
sections.summary: The Public Prosecutor's decision to charge should not depend on public opinion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Public Prosecutor's decision to charge should not depend on public opinion.

sections.label: Judge facing conflicting pressure
sections.summary: The speaker asks how a judge reacts to conflicting sources of pressure, and says the law allows comments only after proceedings are over.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: How then is the judge to react in the face of all these conflicting sources of pressure?

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: That is why our law provides that you can make your comments, just wait for the proceedings to be over.

sections.label: Keeping system free from influence
sections.summary: The speaker urges keeping the system as pristine as possible and protecting it from outside influence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Let us keep the system as pristine as possible and protect it from outside influence.

sections.label: Italian court on media hype
sections.summary: Italy's Supreme Court of Cassation observed that unusual hype and international pressure accelerated investigations, hindering the search for substantial truth.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Italy's highest court, the Supreme Court of Cassation, observed that: "Certainly, the unusual hype of the story, caused not only by the dramatic mode of death of a 22-year-old…but also by the nationality of the people involved…and therefore by the international repercussions of the story, caused the investigations to suffer a sudden acceleration, which, in the frantic search for one or more culprits to be delivered to international public opinion, certainly did not facilitate seeking the substantial truth." This is not the type of justice system we want.

sections.label: Reversing burdens requires statute
sections.summary: Reversing burdens must be done statutorily for specific public policy reasons, with guilt determined through tested evidence in Court.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: If you want to reverse burdens, that has to be done statutorily for specific public policy reasons.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It is for these reasons that we have a process for determining guilt or innocence before the Courts where evidence is tested and scrutinised, where unreliable evidence is excluded, and where the Court makes findings based on a detailed analysis of the law and facts.

sections.label: UK sub judice contempt bar
sections.summary: The United Kingdom has set a higher bar before a person can be found guilty of sub judice contempt.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The United Kingdom (UK) has set a higher bar before you can find a person guilty of sub judice contempt.

sections.label: Courts reject UK approach
sections.summary: Singapore Courts rejected the UK approach partly because the UK position is subject to the ECHR, and clause 3(4) exempts Government statements in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Our Courts have expressly rejected the approach taken in the UK, inter alia, for the reason that the UK position has been impacted by it being subject to ECHR.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I now turn to clause 3(4) of the Bill, which says "A person who issues a statement on behalf of the Government will not be liable for sub judice, notwithstanding pending Court proceedings, if it is in the public interest to do so".

sections.label: Clause 14 fair reporting protection
sections.summary: Clause 14 permits fair, accurate, good faith reports of ongoing proceedings published contemporaneously or within a reasonable time, absent contrary law, court order or confidential matters.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Clause 14 of the Bill permits a fair and accurate report of ongoing proceedings that is in good faith; published contemporaneously or within a reasonable time after the proceedings, unless such publication would otherwise be contrary to the law, order of court or relates to confidential matters.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It also provides that there is no liability if the publisher did not know or have reason to believe that the proceedings were pending.

sections.label: Clause 3(1)(a) contempt test
sections.summary: Clause 3(1)(a) makes it contempt to impute improper motives or impugn a Court's integrity, propriety or impartiality, and requires a risk to public confidence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Clause 3(1)(a) provides that it is contempt of Court to impute improper motives, or impugns the integrity, propriety or impartiality of any Court, and, so, this is conjunctive – if what you do or publish poses a risk that public confidence in the administration of justice will be undermined.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, you have got to show that the statements impugned the integrity, propriety or impartiality, or imputed improper motives, and you also have to show that there was a risk that public confidence and the administration of justice would be impacted.

sections.label: Repeated false statements study
sections.summary: A Vanderbilt-led study found repeated false statements made participants later believe them true even when they knew better.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: There is a recent psychological study led by a Vanderbilt University researcher.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It showed that false statements which were repeated even when the participants knew better caused participants to later believe the statements were true.

sections.label: Bill's contempt risk test
sections.summary: The Bill uses a risk test for contempt, and its clauses on substantive elements are the one change to current law.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In the Bill, the test is "risk." The different heads of contempt, clauses 3 and 4, what amounts to contempt, the Bill sets out the law as it stands now.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This is the one change to the current law in the clauses on the substantive elements of contempt.

sections.label: Survey on trust in Courts
sections.summary: A Ministry survey found 92% trusted the legal system and over 90% had confidence in the State Courts.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: My Ministry conducted a survey recently on how Singaporeans view our Courts.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: And 92% said they had trust and confidence in our legal system; 96% agreed that Singapore was governed by rule of law.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: More than 90% had confidence in the fair administration of justice by the State Courts; agreed that the State Courts independently carried out justice according to the law; and agreed that the State Courts administered justice with integrity.

sections.label: World Bank rule of law ranking
sections.summary: The World Bank ranked Singapore in the 95th percentile for the rule of law.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The World Bank ranked us in the 95th percentile for the rule of law.

sections.label: Clauses on judges and contempt
sections.summary: Clauses 16 and 17 cover reports on judges' conduct and disqualification applications, and imputing improper motives posing risk is contempt.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Clause 16 allows a report to be made to the Chief Justice or relevant authorities on the judges' conduct.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Similarly, clause 17 allows any aggrieved party to file a case or application in Court to seek the disqualification of a judge.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Weighing the importance of maintaining the sanctity and reputation of the Judiciary, we have decided that it should be contempt if one imputes improper motives, impugns the integrity, propriety or impartiality of a Court; and that poses a risk of undermining public confidence in the Judiciary.

sections.label: Real risk versus integrity
sections.summary: The speaker asks why not keep the common law's real risk test, wanting the Judiciary's integrity pristine.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Members may say, yes, but why not the current layer of protection as in the common law, which is "real risk"?

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: I want to make sure that the integrity of the Judiciary is pristine.

sections.label: Singapore International Arbitration Centre in Asia
sections.summary: The Singapore International Arbitration Centre is now the top arbitration body in Asia.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Look at the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC).

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It is now the top arbitration body in Asia.

sections.label: British High Commission scandalising judiciary statement
sections.summary: The British High Commission issued a statement urging Singapore and other countries to abolish scandalising the judiciary.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The balancing will be influenced by the culture and values of the particular community… The result of the balancing process will necessarily reflect the court's assessment of society's values." Hon Members, let me now turn to what the British High Commission said last week, and I will deal with that.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It appears that on 12 August 2016, the British High Commission issued a statement, and I quote: "The UK will continue to urge Singapore and all countries which retain 'scandalising the judiciary' to abolish it." This is surprising.

sections.label: Ministry of Foreign Affairs contacts High Commissioner
sections.summary: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs asked the British High Commissioner about the comment, which he said was not specific to Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs contacted the British High Commission and asked the High Commissioner what this was all about.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: He said that the comment was made by his press office in response to a question posed by Reuters and was not specific to Singapore.

sections.label: UK Law Commission Report 2012
sections.summary: The UK Law Commission Report of 2012 recommended abolishing this offence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The UK Law Commission Report of 2012 recommended the abolishment of this offence for the following reasons.

sections.label: Judges say judiciary less respected
sections.summary: Almost two-thirds of judges said the judiciary is respected by society less than 10 years ago.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Almost two-thirds of all the judges (62%) said that members of the judiciary are respected by society less than they were 10 years ago.

sections.label: Decline in judicial morale in UK
sections.summary: Decline in judicial morale is reflected in increasing difficulty recruiting and retaining judges, especially senior judges, in the UK.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Decline in judicial morale has been reflected in the increasing difficulty in recruiting and retaining judges, especially senior judges, in the UK.

sections.label: Britain standards comparison decision
sections.summary: The speaker says changes in Britain have not been for the better and Singapore has decided not to follow that way.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The changes in Britain have not been for the better.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: And we have decided, consciously, not to go that way.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We are upholding standards that have gone down in Britain and have led to a loss of respect and coarsening of society.

sections.label: Clause 12 contempt maximum punishments
sections.summary: Clause 12 sets maximum contempt punishments: Court of Appeal and High Court up to $100,000 fine or three years' imprisonment, or both; other Courts lower.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: First, clause 12 of the Bill sets out the maximum punishment for committing contempt.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Clause 12 sets out what the maximum punishments are.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Court of Appeal and High Court can punish contempt with a fine not exceeding $100,000, or not exceeding three years of imprisonment, or both.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: For other Courts, the maximum punishments are lower, namely, a fine not exceeding $20,000, or not exceeding 12 months' imprisonment, or both.

sections.label: Court of Appeal contempt sentence
sections.summary: Earlier this year the Court of Appeal sentenced a man to eight months' imprisonment for disobeying a Court order and failing to pay.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Earlier this year, the Court of Appeal sentenced a man to eight months' imprisonment for disobeying a Court order to pay his wife maintenance and for failing to pay her share of matrimonial assets in divorce proceedings.

sections.label: Contempt committed in Singapore
sections.summary: The Bill provides that contempt of Court can be committed in Singapore even if some acts occurred outside Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Second, the Bill provides that contempt of Court can be committed in Singapore, even if some of the acts had occurred outside Singapore.

sections.label: Clause 13 Attorney-General publisher direction
sections.summary: Clause 13 permits the Attorney-General to apply to the High Court for leave to direct a publisher to not publish or stop publishing contemptuous material.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Clause 13 of the Bill permits the Attorney-General (AG) to apply to the High Court for leave to direct a publisher to not publish, or stop publishing, material that is contemptuous.

sections.label: Clause 18 innocent publication defence
sections.summary: There is a defence of innocent publication or distribution under clause 18 of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Fourthly, there is a defence of innocent publication or distribution under clause 18 of the Bill.

sections.label: Trust in legal system survey
sections.summary: A survey found 92% of Singaporeans trust the legal system and 96% agree Singapore is governed by the rule of law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In a survey conducted at the end of last year, 92% of Singaporeans have trust and confidence in our legal system, and 96% of Singaporeans agree that Singapore is governed by the rule of law.

sections.label: Bill defines scandalising the Court
sections.summary: The Bill sets out what amounts to scandalising the Court, namely comments that can erode public confidence in the judicial system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The Bill sets out what would amount to "scandalising the Court".

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: These are such comments that can erode the public's confidence in the judicial system, if not checked.

sections.label: Protecting confidence in justice administration
sections.summary: The Bill protects public confidence in the administration of justice by disallowing allegations of judicial bias, with appeals available, and suggests a real risk test.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: What the Bill seeks to protect is the public's confidence in the administration of justice by disallowing allegations that the judge is privately motivated or partial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Furthermore, if you think the judgment is wrong, an appeal can be filed if the client decides to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It seems to suggest that the test for when an allegation scandalises the Court should be that there is a "real risk" that the allegation or assertion scandalises the Court rather than a risk that the allegation or assertion scandalises the Court.

sections.label: Penal Code negligence offences wording
sections.summary: Penal Code offences for negligent or rash acts endangering lives do not require real negligence, real rashness or really endangering, as section 336 shows.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In the Penal Code, the offences that criminalise negligent or rash acts that endanger lives and safety do not say, there must be "real negligence" or "real rashness" or even "really endangering".

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Instead, the statutes read like this: "Whoever does any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others, shall be punished…" under section 336, Penal Code, Chapter 224.

sections.label: Bill tools preserve Court repute
sections.summary: The Bill gives effective tools to preserve the repute of the Courts in a dynamic Court room setting where time is of the essence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In a dynamic Court room setting, Madam, time is of the essence, cases do go on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: This Bill gives effective tools to preserve the repute of our Courts.

sections.label: Protecting courts and rule of law
sections.summary: Protection can be afforded to the courts to preserve the rule of law and the good standing of the Singapore Judiciary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Yes, we can afford protection to the courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: We have to, in order to preserve the rule of law and the good standing of the Singapore Judiciary.

sections.label: Court reputation freefall risk
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether accumulated risks could cause a freefall of the Court's reputation among Singaporeans, and supports the Bill to preserve the Judiciary's repute.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: What if one day those risks add up and cause a freefall of the Court's reputation in the eyes of Singaporeans?

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: We are today preserving the repute of the Judiciary and I support the Bill.

sections.label: WP rejects Bill's key effects
sections.summary: The WP rejects the Bill, citing lowered scandalising threshold, muzzling of pending case discussion with Government immunity, and possible state machinery intimidation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The WP rejects the Bill as we reject several of its key effects, such as: (a) unnecessarily lowering the threshold for what amounts to scandalising the Courts; (b) muzzling discussion on pending Court cases while giving the Government immunity to say what it deems fit, however prejudicial; and (c) the potential utilisation of the state machinery to intimidate Singaporeans who, in good faith, wish to discuss current affairs.

sections.label: Minister acknowledges clause 3(1)(a) change
sections.summary: The Minister acknowledged a clear change under clause 3(1)(a), where scandalising the Court includes publishing matter imputing improper motives and posing a risk to public confidence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: According to the Minister for Law before the Sitting, he has said that the law on contempt will remain broadly the same.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I am glad that today the Minister has acknowledged that at least one clear change is being made under the Bill in relation to clause 3(1)(a), where it is stated that a person scandalises the Court if he publishes any matter or does any act that imputes improper motives or alleges impropriety of any Court and that publication or act poses a risk that public confidence in the administration of justice would be undermined.

sections.label: Bill lowers contempt bar
sections.summary: By requiring only a risk that public confidence in the administration of justice would be undermined, the Bill has lowered the bar for contempt of Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: By changing the test to requiring the offending statement or act to carry just a risk that public confidence in the administration of justice would be undermined, the Bill has lowered the bar for contempt of Court.

sections.label: Government-only sub judice exception
sections.summary: Clause 3(4) introduces a new sub judice contempt exception usable only by the Government for statements it believes necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, clause 3(4) introduces a new exception to sub judice contempt which can only be used by the Government, and I would like to quote the phrasing, "A statement by a person on behalf of the Government about an aspect of a pending Court proceeding is not contempt if the Government believes that such statement is necessary in the public interest." What is this exception for?

sections.label: Coroner's inquiry Government statement illustration
sections.summary: Illustration 1 covers a Government statement about circumstances leading to a death while the Coroner's inquiry into that death is pending.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Illustration 1 covers a Government statement about the circumstances leading to the death of a person when the Coroner's inquiry into the death is pending.

sections.label: Contempt accusations and blanket licence
sections.summary: The passage asks whether he faces contempt accusations and wants blanket licence, making the Government sole subjective judge.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Has he been facing accusations that he has acted in contempt of Court and wants blanket licence to say what he likes?

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This means that the Government will be sole judge of what is necessary; the test is subjective and the Government's assessment is not open to challenge.

sections.label: Minister contempt and AG directions
sections.summary: It states ministers are not above contempt law, and the Bill gives the AG non-publication directions with fines or imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A Minister of the Government is not above the law and if a statement made by him is calculated to prejudice the fair trial of an accused person and if the risk of interference with the proper administration of justice is a real and grave one, such a contempt will be met with the necessary punishment in order to restrain such conduct." Madam, the present Bill replaces the oversight of the Courts with a subjective test of what the Government believes is necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This is a change in the law which will give the Government practical immunity.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under clause 13, a new power is given to the AG to issue a non-publication direction to the publisher of any matter to refrain from publishing it if the AG is satisfied that it is in the public interest to do so.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Disobedience to such a direction carries a fine of up $20,000 or imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both.

sections.label: High Court must grant leave
sections.summary: Under clause 13(7), once the AG shows certain conditions are met, the High Court must grant leave for a non-publication direction.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: According to clause 13(7), once the AG shows that the case satisfies certain conditions, the High Court must grant leave to the AG to issue the non-publication direction.

sections.label: Fair trial and debate concerns
sections.summary: The Bill protects fair trial in court proceedings, but the speaker fears it may unduly restrict legitimate debate on public matters.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the situation where they are involved in a Court proceeding, this Bill protects them and ensures they are given a fair trial that is untainted by public discussion on the case at hand.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Hence, while I am not fundamentally opposed to codifying the law of contempt into the statute, I am concerned that the current provisions of the Bill may unintentionally result in undue restriction on legitimate debate of important matters that affect the public.

sections.label: Lower test and AGC power
sections.summary: Two changes are noted: lowering the scandalising test from real risk to risk, and giving the AGC more contempt power.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As I understand, there are two main changes to note, specifically: first, lowering the test for scandalising the Court from the previous term, "real risk" to just "risk"; and second, investing more power in AGC in this Bill with regard to contempt of Court.

sections.label: Public discussion led reviews
sections.summary: Public discussion of Dominique's case led SAF safety reviews, and outcry over Benjamin Lim led police and education procedure reviews.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Public discussion on Dominique's case had, in part, led to the Singapore Armed Forces reviewing and improving their safety management.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Considerable public outcry and concern over the death of Benjamin Lim had also led the Ministry of Education and the Singapore Police Force to review their procedures when the Police conduct interviews with young persons.

sections.label: Contempt of Court punishment
sections.summary: The Bill prescribes a maximum punishment for contempt of Court of up to $100,000 and/or three years' imprisonment, which the speaker calls harsh and disproportionate for a non-violent offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under the Bill, the prescribed maximum punishment for contempt of Court of up to $100,000 and/or a term of imprisonment of not more than three years is exceedingly harsh and disproportionate for a non-violent offence.

sections.label: Sub judice real and grave risk
sections.summary: In that case it was held that a statement is sub judice only when the risk of interference with the proper administration of justice is real and grave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In that case, it was held that a statement would only be sub judice when the risk of interference with the proper administration of justice was a real and grave one.

sections.label: Civil society campaigns and sub judice
sections.summary: The speaker welcomes the Minister's statement that a civil society group campaigning to abolish the death penalty would not be seen as sub judice even during a related Court case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Within civil society, certain ongoing campaigns aim to protect the interest of the common people, even if they are minorities or belong to marginalised groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am very glad to hear from the Minister that, if a civil society group that advocates the abolishment of the death penalty and there was a Court case that sought to repeal the death sentence, their campaign would not be seen as sub judice.

sections.label: Government statements exempt from contempt
sections.summary: Clause 3(4) exempts Government statements on pending Court proceedings if the Government believes they are necessary in the public interest, which the speaker questions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Bill states in clause 3(4) that a statement made by a person on behalf of the Government on a pending Court proceeding is exempt from contempt of Court if the Government believes such a statement is necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While I recognise the importance of having the Government make statements when necessary in the public interest, this clause seems to imply that the Government would be the final arbiter of facts and what constitute public interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I believe it is necessary to remind ourselves that it is the Court, not the Government, that is the ultimate arbiter of facts in all disputes, both among civilians, and between the Government and the people.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Given that the Government's statement undoubtedly wields great impact on the people, will its comments pending Court proceedings influence witnesses?

sections.label: Defence for public interest individuals
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether individuals should have a public interest defence, what lowering the test changed, and warns that unclear impact will cause public fear of discussing public interest matters.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While this Bill provides opportunities and defence for the Government and the AGC to voice their positions, should there not be provision of a defence for public interest raised by individuals or the common man?

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: What I want to ask is, after lowering the test, what has changed exactly?

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, I have detailed my concerns pertaining to the Administration of Justice (Protection) Bill in my speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There are various clarifications that the Ministry has provided and can provide in layman's terms, so that the public can better understand the impact of the Bill on their daily lives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Failure to do so will inevitably cause undue augmented fear in the public to discuss matters of public interest, in case they are accused of sub judice.

sections.label: More and earlier consultations
sections.summary: More consultations and earlier consultations would help make people better informed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: More consultations and earlier consultations would help make people better informed.

sections.label: Contempt of Court Bill framework
sections.summary: The new Bill sets out the definition of contempt of Court, defences available, and a framework of punishments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The new Bill sets out the definition of contempt of Court, defences available, as well as a framework of punishments that can be meted out.

sections.label: Industrial Arbitration Court judgments coverage
sections.summary: A labour MP had hoped IAC judgments, presided by a High Court judge, would be covered in the Bill's definition of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: First, speaking as a labour Member of Parliament and practitioner of employment and industrial relations law, I had hoped that judgments awarded by the Industrial Arbitration Court (IAC) which is presided by a High Court judge would be covered within the definition of "Court" in section 2 of this Bill to give full force and weight to ensure compliance of the judgment.

sections.label: Industrial Relations Act contempt procedure
sections.summary: The Industrial Relations Act provides a two-step contempt procedure that the MP submits can be better aligned with the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Although the Industrial Relations Act does provide for a specific procedure to follow for contempt proceedings, it is a two-step process which, I submit, can be better aligned with what is provided in this Bill and made more robust, effective and speedy.

sections.label: Tribunals left out of Bill
sections.summary: Decisions by tribunals such as the Small Claims Tribunal and others were left out of the Bill's ambit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Second, decisions and judgments by tribunals, such as the Small Claims Tribunal, Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal as well as the upcoming Employment Claims Tribunal, have also been left out of the ambit of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Taking into cognisance the fact that there are specific provisions in the respective legislation to address contempt, I submit that a more effective and robust enforcement and deterrence regime, such as those provided in this Bill, would have made enforcement of tribunal orders even more efficacious, expeditious and economical for the laymen to utilise such tribunals to resolve their disputes.

sections.label: Benjamin Lim suicide case
sections.summary: The suicide of 14-year-old Benjamin Lim in January is still fresh in the public's minds.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The suicide of 14-year-old Benjamin Lim in January this year is still fresh in the minds of many members of the public.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It was only five months ago on 1 March this year that Minister Shanmugam laid out the facts of the case in response to online statements and reported comments about the events leading to the suicide.

sections.label: Broad meaning of publish
sections.summary: The meaning of publish is so broad it covers personal electronic communication and social messaging between friends.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The meaning of "publish" here is so broad that it covers personal electronic communication and social messaging between friends.

sections.label: Clause 4 Government immunity
sections.summary: Clause 4 gives the Government blanket immunity from sub judice contempt, illustrated by statements on a person's death during a Coroner's inquiry.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: To make matters worse, clause 4 gives the Government blanket immunity from sub judice contempt.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Illustration 1 of this immunity states that "a statement made by a person on behalf of the Government factually describing the events and circumstances relating to and leading up to the death of a person (such as the acts of public officials when a Coroner's inquiry into the person's death is pending) which the Government believes is necessary to address inaccurate and incorrect public allegations, is not contempt of Court".

sections.label: Father opposes unnecessary law
sections.summary: A father says he expects trust to express fair criticism on cases relating to his sons' safety, so the law is unnecessary and silences discussion.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Above all, as a father who would entrust my two sons to our education system and then the armed forces, I expect the same level of trust to be accorded to me by the Government to be able to express fair criticism and ask fair questions on cases that relate to my sons' safety.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I, therefore, do not see the need for this law to be enacted.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In fact, this law is not only unnecessary, it also gives the Executive unprecedented powers that would silence public discussion on the facts of cases of great public interest.

sections.label: Bill called overreaction
sections.summary: The speaker says the process righted and clarified doubts and affirmed trust, so the Bill is an overreaction.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It was a process that righted and clarified the doubts and affirmed trust.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This is why this Bill is an overreaction.

sections.label: Feared effects of Bill
sections.summary: The speaker fears the Bill is unnecessary, counter-productive and subversive of trust, and asks that it not be hasty.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This is what I fear would happen when this Bill becomes law.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It is utterly unnecessary, counter-productive and ultimately subversive of trust between the Government and the people.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If the Government must insist on pushing through this Bill, then, at the very least, we should not be hasty about it.

sections.label: Departure from Shadrake test
sections.summary: The speaker's problem is that the Bill departs from the High Court and Court of Appeal in Alan Shadrake, which held the test is real risk.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: My only problem with this is that it departs from the High Court and the Court of Appeal in Alan Shadrake, which was the case I just mentioned earlier.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Court of Appeal held that the appropriate test is that of "real risk".

sections.label: Four questions on risk
sections.summary: The speaker asks why the House would depart from the Apex Court's rule and whether a lower risk threshold is being adopted.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One, could the Minister explain why the House or the Ministry would like to statutorily depart from a legal rule followed by the Apex Court?

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Two, are we moving backwards to a test which has a lower threshold by only using the word "risk"?

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Three, are we saying that a "risk" will be established if there is just a small likelihood?

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Four, can contempt be established where there is only a remote or fanciful possibility that public confidence in the administration of justice might be undermined?

sections.label: Meaning of word prejudges
sections.summary: A member asks why the word "prejudges" is used in clause 3(1)(b)(i) and whether it has a specific meaning there.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: That puts my mind at ease as far as that clause is concerned.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I only ask one question and, that is, why the word "prejudges" is used in clause 3(1)(b)(i), and whether there is specific meaning to that particular word in the context of this clause.

sections.label: Threshold and public opinion clarification
sections.summary: A member seeks clarification that the test involves prejudgement plus actual prejudice or real risk, and that the public may express strong good faith opinions on pending cases.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In short, it puts the threshold far lower than even "risk".

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, if I may get a clarification, Madam, from the Minister that the real test is not just prejudgement, but prejudgement and actual prejudice or real risk of prejudice or interference.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Can I also get a clarification from the Minister, Madam, that members of the public can express strong opinions in good faith about pending cases as long as the dissemination of these opinions are not calculated to propagate a particular view which would cause actual prejudice or a real risk of prejudice?

sections.label: Statements by press secretaries and Ministries
sections.summary: A member asks what happens if a press secretary publishes a statement out of turn or a Ministry makes a statement most Singaporeans disagree with.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If I may ask, what happens if a press secretary publishes a statement out of turn on a different matter, or if a Ministry makes a statement that it believes is necessary in the public interest but most Singaporeans disagree, and if an Organ of State, such as the Attorney-General or Auditor-General also thinks otherwise?

sections.label: Recourse for tainted court proceedings
sections.summary: A member asks the Minister to clarify whether the Bill allows recourse for a person with good faith suspicion that a court proceeding is tainted.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Some of us believe that perhaps that exception could be proposed when we suggested an amendment in that context.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But may I just ask if the Minister can clarify that even if there is no reciprocal public affairs interest exception that people can rely on, that the Bill, as it currently stands, allows for avenues through which a member of the public can seek recourse if he or she has a good faith suspicion that a Court proceeding is tainted by impropriety or bias?

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Most importantly, in my mind, is because it is a long time coming.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It was first outlined in 2010 at the Opening of the Legal Year by the former Chief Justice.

sections.label: Scandalising the Court cases cited
sections.summary: A member cites cases held by the current Chief Justice and other Justices of Appeal, especially the Alan Shadrake case.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The first is that when we look at the cases that the current Chief Justice and other Justices of Appeal have held, especially in cases like Alan Shadrake, the most recent case for scandalising the Court, the High Court case went up to the Court of Appeal.

sections.label: Justice Quentin Loh on debate
sections.summary: Justice Quentin Loh said judges have no interest in stifling public interest debate, including debate about judges' conduct.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These are the words from Justice Quentin Loh again from the High Court in the Alan Shadrake case.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: He said that judges have no interest in stifling debate and, indeed, debate in the public interest, including of judges' conduct, that they are constitutionally bound to ensure that every citizen has a right to engage in such robust debate, and, in fact, especially debate is critical if it is about judges.

sections.label: Disobedience of Court orders
sections.summary: The Bill signals that disobedience of Court orders will not be tolerated, especially by recalcitrant judgment debtors, affecting real people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Three, people, real people are significantly affected when orders of Court are not complied with and this Bill sends a strong signal that disobedience of Court orders will not be tolerated, especially by recalcitrant judgment debtors.

sections.label: Government public interest exception
sections.summary: Concerns were raised about the Government exception for public interest statements, which is circumscribed by what is necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I note that there have been concerns raised about the exception for the Government to make statements necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I would highlight that though there are legal limits to these rights and the Government cannot just say anything that it wants, it is circumscribed by what is necessary in the public interest, and the illustrations in the proposed provisions also provide guidance on this.

sections.label: Deterrent effect for judgment debtors
sections.summary: Putting existing law into statute and raising maximum punishment creates greater deterrence and protects vulnerable parties like women and children.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: By putting the existing law clearly into statute and by raising the prescribed maximum punishment which can be imposed by the State Courts and the Family Courts, this creates a greater deterrent effect and sends a strong signal to recalcitrant judgment debtors.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I believe that the Bill will ensure that vulnerable parties like women and children, who are not receiving maintenance that they are entitled to, will receive the full protection of the justice system.

sections.label: Enforcement plans and Bill support
sections.summary: The speaker asks if the Ministry of Law has further enforcement plans, supports the Bill, but says it extends extraordinary powers to the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Does the Ministry of Law have any further plans to make enforcement of Court orders more effective?

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding my request for clarification, Mdm Speaker, I support this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But rather than to merely codify the common law on contempt in Singapore, this Bill threatens to upset this delicate balance by extending extraordinary powers to the Government.

sections.label: Clause 3 stringent test
sections.summary: The Minister's Second Reading speech shows clause 3 envisages a more stringent test than the real risk test for scandalising the Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In view of the Minister's Second Reading speech, it is clear that clause 3 does, indeed, envisage a more stringent test than the "real risk" test in cases of scandalising the Court.

sections.label: Undefined term prejudgment
sections.summary: The term prejudgment is introduced but is not defined in the interpretation section of the Bill, compounding ambiguity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Compounding this ambiguity is the introduction of the term "prejudgment", a term which is curiously not defined in the interpretation section of the Bill.

sections.label: Purpose of sub judice contempt
sections.summary: Concerns raised over the sub judice contempt clause should return Members to the purpose of such laws: protecting the right to a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Furthermore, the concerns many Singaporeans have raised over the clause on sub judice contempt ought to bring Members back to the fundamental purpose of sub judice contempt laws in the first place, which is to protect the right to a fair trial.

sections.label: Common law versus this Bill
sections.summary: Common law would suffice for egregious sub judice contempt, and the Bill gives the AG a potentially overwhelming role with a low standard of proof.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Relying on the common law to address sub judice contempt in egregious cases of sub judice would more than suffice, so as to preserve a healthy balance between freedom of speech and public confidence in the administration of justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There is simply no overwhelming reason to pass this Bill when Singapore's experience with sub judice contempt, in particular, has not compromised the conduct of fair trials.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: With the passage of this Bill into law, the Government, and specifically the AG, by virtue of clause 13, has a potentially overwhelming role in determining the balance between freedom of speech and the administration of justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Worse, the AG only has to prove a prima facie case of contempt – an exceedingly low standard of proof.

sections.label: Arrestable contempt and police powers
sections.summary: Making sub judice contempt arrestable via clause 22 and giving Police confiscation powers appears targeted at civil society activists who challenge the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Even worse, making sub judice contempt arrestable by way of clause 22 and thereby giving the Police powers to confiscate personal computers, amongst other things, appears to be specifically targeted at civil society activists who are not afraid to challenge the Government and who play their part in serving Singapore by contributing to a diverse public space of voices and views.

sections.label: Fines and imprisonment terms compared
sections.summary: The Bill's $100,000 fine and three-year term are questioned against Alan Shadrake's six weeks and $20,000 fine for the worst scandalising contempt case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To conclude, Mdm Speaker, how much confidence is one supposed to take from a Bill which criminalises contempt by a fine of up to $100,000 at the High Court and a three-year imprisonment term, when the Court of Appeal in Alan Shadrake affirmed a sentence of six weeks imprisonment and a $20,000 fine in what it called, and I quote, "the worst case of scandalising contempt that has hitherto come before the Singapore Courts", unquote.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If Alan Shadrake's stands for the worst case of scandalising contempt in Singapore's 51-year history, how can the Government justify increasing the prison term and fine by such a wide margin?

sections.label: Fines for other contempt scenarios
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the Government envisages higher fines and imprisonment terms for other contempt scenarios, such as sub judice contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Does the Government envisage a higher quantum of fines and imprisonment terms for other contempt scenarios, like sub judice contempt, for example?

sections.label: Exception for Government statements
sections.summary: Clause 3(4) protects Government representatives' statements on pending proceedings if believed necessary in the public interest, with no similar exception for ordinary people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Clause 3(4) of the Bill carves out an exception for Government representatives making statements on pending Court proceedings, protecting them from accusations of contempt of Court as long as that statement made is believed by the Government as "necessary in the public interest".

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Their contention is this: as a matter of principle, why then is there no similar exception being carved out to protect the common person?

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: What they are asking for is a much more obvious signal in the Bill that communicates protection will also be given for fair criticisms on public affairs made by ordinary people who may also have good reason to believe what they say could be construed by a Court as just and necessary in the public interest as a statement from the Government.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Another controversy for them in this clause is that phrase "if the Government believes that such statement is necessary in the public interest".

sections.label: Youth worry over Executive power
sections.summary: Kids worry about the resilience of Singapore's political system and ask whether a legal check and balance exists to protect people from an Executive branch gone wrong.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And against the backdrop of freak presidential elections and crazy referendums elsewhere in the world, it is not surprising the kids worry over the resilience of our own political system in a future situation of similar nuttiness.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: They just want to know that if it is, indeed, going to be the Executive branch solely determining what is necessary in the "public interest", is there a legal check and balance to protect the people from an Executive branch gone wrong?

sections.label: Free speech versus fair trial
sections.summary: The Bill is essentially about the tension between the public interest in every man's right to free speech and the public interest in every man's right to a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Like this Bill itself, it is essentially about the tension between the public interest of every man's right to free speech with the public interest of every man's right to a fair trial, unsullied by someone's prejudicial campaigning in the media.

sections.label: Youth-centric translation of Bill
sections.summary: Youths are uncertain about the definition of "prejudices" and whether a single prejudicial WhatsApp message could be construed as mass publication of contempt, prompting a request for a youth-centric translation of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: They are still uncertain about what is the definition of "prejudices" and, since the definition of "publications" is so wide, they are uncertain about whether their one single "prejudicial" WhatsApp message communicated to just one other friend could be construed as a mass publication of contempt.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, their anxieties sparked me to request the Ministry of Law create a youth-centric translation of the Bill that reads less as a legal document and more like something written for 16-year-olds to hear.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It will be very helpful; and an accompanying youth-centric set of frequently asked questions will help.

sections.label: Youth indifference to Bill debate
sections.summary: The majority's indifference should disturb us more than anger, and passing the Bill without inspiring much debate or discussion with youths is not a win for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If I am thinking about what kind of political education and political will our young need to help Singapore thrive, I would say the majority's reaction of indifference should disturb us far more than the former's anger.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am not convinced it is a win for Singapore if we pass this Bill without inspiring much debate or having much discussion with the majority of our youths.

sections.label: Sedition Act and kiasu avoidance
sections.summary: The Sedition Act protects against racist and religious hate speech but dovetails with kiasu culture, letting people avoid all deep talk about race and religion in case they get into trouble.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Sedition Act, for instance, gives us protection from racist and religious hate speech but it also dovetails with our country's kiasu culture and let many kiasu people to take the kiasu route of simply avoiding all talk about issues of race and religion at any deep and meaningful level in case they get into trouble.

sections.label: Who is the Government
sections.summary: Clause 3(4) says a Government statement about a pending Court proceeding is not contempt if the Government believes it necessary in the public interest, and the Minister is asked to clarify who exactly is the "Government".

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First point, clause 3(4) of the Bill says "a statement made by a person on behalf of the Government about a Court proceeding that is pending is not contempt of Court if the Government believes that such statement is necessary in the public interest".

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Could the Minister clarify who exactly is the "Government" that is positioned as the final arbiter of what is necessary in the public interest?

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Is it the Executive branch, that is, Cabinet and the President: the Judiciary of the Courts; or the Legislative branch, that is, Parliament?

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And will it be the single belief of an individual or the collective belief of that branch that will be the determiner of "what is necessary in the public interest"?

sections.label: Public affairs exception request
sections.summary: The speaker urges the Minister for Law to reconsider a public affairs exception for smaller individuals paralleling protections for bigger institutions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Lastly, I urge the Minister for Law to reconsider creating a space in this Bill for a discussion of public affairs exception for the smaller individual that parallels the protections currently given to the bigger institution.

sections.label: Assurance for statement makers
sections.summary: The speaker asks for assurance that fair, responsible statements in the public interest without real risk to justice will not be contempt.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Give both the Singaporeans who work for the ground and the Singaporeans who work for the Government that same powerful assurance that as long as their statements are made fairly and responsibly, in the service of public interest, without real risk or seriously prejudicing the course of justice, they will not be held in contempt.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And if making even a gesture of that exception in the Ministry's opinion is not tenable or even really necessary, then could the Minister explain fully why that is so?

sections.label: Bigger institution reassuring smaller
sections.summary: The speaker says the bigger institution must lead in reassuring the smaller that they are heard and their interests protected.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, no matter how well-intentioned or benign the bigger entity perceives itself to be, it must see that the smaller will always struggle with some degree of anxiety in navigating the rules of engagement with the bigger.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, whilst us individual citizens have a responsibility to own our side of the conversation and navigate our own fears and bias about the bigger institution, the bigger must take the lead to reassure the smaller that they are heard and their interests will be protected.

sections.label: Clause 3(1)(a)(2) scandalising liability
sections.summary: The speaker notes clause 3(1)(a)(2) provides liability for intentionally publishing matter posing a risk to public confidence in justice.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I appreciate your patience, Mdm Speaker, with my use of slang.

sentences.speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I look forward to the Minister's clarifications and fair consideration of the proposed amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Clause 3(1)(a)(2) of this Bill provides for liability for anyone who scandalises the Court by intentionally publishing any matter or doing any act that includes posing "a risk that public confidence in administration of justice may be undermined".

sections.label: Omission of real risk
sections.summary: The speaker says omitting the word real from clause 3(1)(a) makes the contempt bar significantly lower than the real risk test.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Taking a more liberal attitude towards the law of contempt of Court than the High Court, the Court of Appeal that a 'small likelihood' of risk would 'merely be a technical' contempt that may not even attract any sanction at all." The proposed wording in clause 3(1)(a) provides for "a risk that public confidence in administration of justice may be undermined" and not just a real risk.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I think the omission of the word "real" – which I now understand is intentional – makes the bar for contempt significantly lower than the real risk test.

sections.label: Clause 3(b) and 3(4)
sections.summary: The speaker finds clause 3(b) patronising to judges and notes clause 3(4) exempts Government statements believed necessary in the public sphere.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I find the provisions in clause 3(b) to be extremely patronising to our judges.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I next refer to clause 3(4) which provides that a statement made by a person on behalf of the Government about the subject matter of or an issue in a Court proceeding that is pending is not contempt under section 1(b) if the Government believes that such statement is necessary in the public sphere.

sections.label: Clause 12(a) maximum penalties
sections.summary: Clause 12(a) of the Bill provides maximum imprisonment of three years and maximum fines of $100,000, or both.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Clause 12(a) of the Bill provides for maximum imprisonment of three years and maximum fines of $100,000, or with both such fine and imprisonment together.

sections.label: Bill penalties higher than cases
sections.summary: The Bill's proposed maximum penalties are significantly higher than the sentences awarded in the three cited cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Comparing the sentences awarded in the three cases I cited, with the proposed punishment in the Bill, it is clear the maximum sentences provided in the Bill are significantly higher – $20,000 or $25,000 fine compared to the proposed maximum fine of $100,000; jail of three months compared to the proposed maximum imprisonment of three years.

sections.label: Contempt offences arrestable status
sections.summary: The passage states it is not necessary to make contempt of Court offences arrestable offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This is most peculiar, given the nature of contempt of Court offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It is not necessary at all to make contempt of Court offences arrestable offences.

sections.label: Maximum penalty on conviction
sections.summary: If convicted, the maximum penalty is a $20,000 fine or up to 12 months' imprisonment, or both.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If convicted, a maximum penalty is a fine of $20,000 or up to 12 months' imprisonment, or both.

sections.label: Clause 13(7) proof standard
sections.summary: Clause 13(7) mandates the High Court must allow the Government's application if a prima facie case standard is met.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: To make matters worse, clause 13(7) mandates that the High Court must allow the Government's application if it is satisfied that the standard of proof of prima facie case has been met.

sections.label: Clause 13 gagging order effects
sections.summary: Clause 13 gives the Government a low standard of proof, the defendant a higher one, and makes non-compliance an arrestable offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In short, according to clause 13 of the Bill, the Government in proposing to deprive the defendant of his right to defend himself before the Court makes the decision, gives the Government a low standard of proof to help the Government achieve what is effectively a gagging order, allows the defendant a higher standard of proof when he applies to set aside the order and, finally, making his failure to comply with such an order an arrestable offence punishable by up to 12 months' imprisonment or a fine of $20,000, or both.

sections.label: One-sided Bill, no redress
sections.summary: The Bill, if passed, would favour the Government entirely, leaving individuals no redress or remedy for wrongful or unfair Government comment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Bill, if passed, will be entirely one-sided in favour of the Government, with no redress or remedy for any individual should the Government make a wrongful or unfair comment to the detriment of the individual.

sections.label: Contempt Bill, free speech concerns
sections.summary: The speaker cites the UK Contempt of Court Act 1981 and says the Bill will curb Singaporeans' free speech and give the Executive and Police new powers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Section 5 of the UK's Contempt of Court Act 1981 provides that: "A publication made as or as part of a discussion in good faith of public affairs, or other matters of general public interest, is not to be treated as a contempt of court under the strict liability rule if the risk of impediment or prejudice to particular legal proceedings is merely incidental to the discussion".

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I have heard the Minister on this section but, respectfully, I am of the view that such a provision will still be helpful to our contempt of Court laws if, indeed, the Government wants to codify our contempt of Court law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I am concerned that this Bill will curb freedom of speech and expression among Singaporeans, in particular, commentary on current issues which may embarrass the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: It also gives the Executive and the Police new powers that they currently do not have, which have a chilling effect on fair criticism and public discussion by Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If enacted, this law runs a very high risk of causing the consequence of undermining the public's trust in the Government.

sections.label: Consolidated law on Court orders
sections.summary: A consolidated written law on disobeying Court orders would make people take such orders more seriously, covering employees and matrimonial disputes.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Having a consolidated piece of written law that sets out the consequences of not obeying Court orders will make people sit up and take Court orders more seriously.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am also heartened that for employees, claims against their employers in the soon to be instituted Employment Claims Tribunal will also have to be taken seriously with these changes.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For those caught in matrimonial disputes, this Bill safeguards the interests of the aggrieved party where a judgment has been passed in favour of them against those tardy spouses who disobey Court orders, such as refusing to pay maintenance in the sum of money ordered by the Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Part 4 of the Bill spells out what does not constitute contempt of Court.

sections.label: Curb lifted after proceedings conclude
sections.summary: The Bill states that the curb is lifted only when Court proceedings have concluded, such as after an appeal is heard or concluded.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the Bill, it is stated that the curb is only lifted when the Court proceedings have concluded, such as after an appeal has been heard or concluded.

sections.label: Complaint channels under clause 16
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the complaint channels to the Chief Justice, Police and other enforcement agencies in clause 16 are the only available ones.

sentences.speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Though clause 16 provides for channels of complaints to the Chief Justice, Police and other enforcement agencies, are these the only available channels?

sections.label: Bill goes beyond consolidation
sections.summary: The speaker and colleagues argue the Bill goes beyond mere consolidation or codification and makes expansive changes to the common law on contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: My colleagues and I argue that this Bill actually goes beyond mere consolidation or codification and makes real expansive changes to the current common law landscape on contempt.

sections.label: Rushed legislation without consultation
sections.summary: The Government decided to rush to legislate with no formal consultative process on the Bill's text before First Reading.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Yet, in this case, the Government has decided to rush to legislate, with no formal consultative process on the text of the Bill prior to its First Reading.

sections.label: Scandalising Judiciary penalties and definition
sections.summary: The Minister discussed UK and New Zealand cases, but no other country prescribes harsh maximum penalties and expansive statutory contempt definitions as the Government seeks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Next, Mdm Speaker, on the issue of scandalising the Judiciary, the Minister for Law has discussed in some detail the cases of the UK and New Zealand, but it does not appear that any other country in the world is currently doing what the Government seeks to do now, which is to prescribe harsh maximum penalties for contempt of Court offences and to codify in statute, in expansive fashion, the definition of contempt of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The expansiveness of it has been elaborated by my colleagues: it comes about as a result of replacing the "real risk" test with merely a "risk" test as well as other points they have touched upon.

sections.label: Justification and sub judice exception
sections.summary: The speaker asks what facts justify the risk to Courts, given high public trust, and notes only the Government enjoys a public interest sub judice exception.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: What facts actually support the view that there is a real risk to the functioning and standing of the Courts so as to justify why we are not acting in accordance with what we see in other jurisdictions?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Given the high trust our population reposes in our Judiciary, as the Law Minister has pointed out, should we not be more confident that the administration of justice in Singapore is made of sterner stuff and is less prone to the risk of being undermined?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
