sentences.text: The one-sidedness of this clause lies in the fact that only the Government enjoys a public interest exception to sub judice and not anyone else involved in the case.

sections.label: Maximum penalties seen as minimum
sections.summary: The speaker fears the maximum penalties in section 12, a $100,000 fine or three years' prison, may be seen as the minimum penalty.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In setting out penalties, I fear that the maximum penalties stipulated in section 12 of a $100,000 fine or up to three years in prison may come to be seen as the minimum penalty in the public mind.

sections.label: Shadrake and Alex Au sentences
sections.summary: The Alan Shadrake case drew six weeks' imprisonment and a $20,000 fine; Alex Au's case drew an $8,000 fine.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The sentence in the Alan Shadrake case was six weeks' imprisonment and a $20,000 fine.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In Alex Au's case, which involves scandalising contempt of the Chief Justice, a fine of $8,000 was meted out.

sections.label: Sub judice laws prevent outside interference
sections.summary: The sub judice laws this Bill largely codifies ensure no outside interference prejudices or obstructs the administration of justice during a person's trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Our sub judice laws, which this Bill largely codifies, serve to ensure that when a person is on trial, no outside interference should come into play to prejudice or obstruct the administration of justice by our judges.

sections.label: Sub judice rules and evidence
sections.summary: Sub judice rules prevent dissemination of possibly erroneous information until evidence is weighed and the Court decides.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Sub judice rules would prevent the dissemination of such possibly erroneous information until the evidence has been properly weighed and the Court has made a decision.

sections.label: Trial by media and fair trial
sections.summary: Public discussion of ongoing cases can interfere with or prejudice a case, compromising an accused person's right to a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: To summarise, while most public discussions of ongoing legal cases are well-meaning, it is possible, in the course of such discussions, that reports can interfere with or prejudice an ongoing case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Such trial by media compromises an accused person's right to a fair trial.

sections.label: Enforcement of the Bill
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the Minister can shed light on the practical enforcement of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: First, is the Minister able to shed light on the practical enforcement of this Bill?

sections.label: Public discussion not stifled
sections.summary: The passage asks how the Minister will ensure public discussion or advocacy on matters of public interest is not unnecessarily stifled.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Could the Minister explain how he will ensure that public discussion or advocacy on matters of public interest is not unnecessarily stifled?

sections.label: Sub judice contempt and due process
sections.summary: Interference with proceedings while trial is ongoing is sub judice contempt, so due process must be respected once a matter is before the Court or Coroner.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Someone might interfere with the proceedings, seek to influence the Court process towards an unjust outcome while the trial is still going on, what we have called sub judice contempt.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: So, it is very important that once a matter is before the Court or the Coroner, that due process is respected and followed.

sections.label: Australian magazine identification case
sections.summary: A 1994 Australian magazine published photos of a man accused of murdering backpackers, and the Supreme Court of New South Wales said this interfered with justice and could have affected witnesses' memory.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: A real example cited in Australia in 1994 when a magazine published photos of a man accused of murdering backpackers.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Identification was an issue and the Supreme Court of New South Wales came forward to say this interfered with the due course of justice and could have skewed the recollection, affected the memory of witnesses.

sections.label: Public interest statement exception
sections.summary: Clause 3(4) creates an exception to sub judice contempt for Government statements it deems necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Once the trial is over, discussion can continue.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It also brings me to clause 3(4) of the Bill, which has an exception to the sub judice contempt provisions under clause 3(1)(b).

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: It creates an exception for situations where the Government issues a statement which it deems necessary in the public interest.

sections.label: Courts assessing necessary Government statements
sections.summary: A Member asks how Courts will assess necessity and scrutinise Executive decisions under clause 3(4).

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Could the Minister share with us on how the Courts will assess what is "necessary" when the Government makes a statement that might otherwise be sub judice?

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Can the Minister advise us how the Courts can act as a check and balance, so that any Executive decision under clause 3(4) can be scrutinised to confirm, as needed, that the decision was, indeed, "necessary" and within the bounds of reasonableness?

sections.label: Trial by media harms
sections.summary: Trial-by-media erodes confidence in the Judiciary and most disadvantages less well-off Singaporeans, so fair trial rights remain important.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: And the negative effects can be subtle, eroding confidence in the Judiciary, so that judgments are less and less respected, undermining the Courts' ability to give a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: And if the justice system is undermined through trial-by-media, it is the least well-off who will be most disadvantaged: (a) Singaporeans whose causes are not glamorous, or who are stigmatised by the public; (b) Singaporeans who do not have big social networks or influential writers on their side; and (c) Singaporeans who do not have a $100,000 budget to pay for advertising, to advocate their position or who are not wealthy enough to buy a private media company with millions of views online.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: In this century, Mdm Speaker, the right to a fair trial is as important as ever for Singaporeans from all walks of life.

sections.label: Clarifying public interest statements
sections.summary: A Member asks for clarity on how the Government decides a statement is necessary in the public interest and whether it can be defined.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Many Members have already spoken about clause 3(4) where the Government can make a statement, which if it deems is necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: While some illustrations are given, can the Minister provide more clarity on how the Government will decide on whether such a statement is necessary in the public interest and whether "public interest" can be defined more clearly in the Bill?

sections.label: Defining real risk
sections.summary: A Member asks the Minister for a more detailed definition of what "real risk" entails under clause 3(1)(b).

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Clause 3(1)(b) prohibits the publication of material which poses a "real risk" of prejudice or interference.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister provide a more detailed definition of what "real risk" entails?

sections.label: Spelling out contempt penalties
sections.summary: A Member suggests spelling out penalties for each form of contempt instead of a catch-all provision for clarity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Lastly, instead of a catch-all provision for penalties, it would be useful if penalties for each form of contempt could be spelt out so that there is better clarity for application.

sections.label: Trust in legal system
sections.summary: A survey showed 92% of Singaporeans trust the legal system and 96% agree Singapore is governed by the rule of law.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: As the Minister for Law said earlier, there is one recent survey that showed that 92% of Singaporeans have trust and confidence in our legal system and 96% of Singaporeans agree that Singapore is governed by the rule of law.

sections.label: Alimony enforcement applications statistics
sections.summary: Since 2009, Courts received about 3,000 annual alimony enforcement applications, mostly from women with custody of children.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Statistically, since 2009, the Courts had received on an annual basis about 3,000 applications for the enforcement of alimony payments from divorcees and the majority of aggrieved parties were women, mostly with custody of children.

sections.label: Contempt punishment and public education
sections.summary: The passage discusses contempt punishment limits, alternative oversight of defaulters' income, and public education on the Bill's purpose and contempt punishments.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: In a scenario where a defaulter is in contempt of Court due to his wanton disobedience of the Court order to pay maintenance to his ex-wife, for instance, the Court can invoke the punishment under section 12 whereby he will be subjected to punishment either by fine, with or without imprisonment, or both.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Although section 12(1) did begin with "Except as otherwise provided in any other written law", it is still not wide enough to capture situations which may not warrant such penal punishment as a fine or custodial sentence or both.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: In the case cited above, perhaps the more appropriate form of punishment may be to make an order for an appointed personnel of the Court, or let us call him a "trusted friend of the Court", to oversee and distribute the defaulter's income, so that all the aggrieved parties receive their payments due in a just and equitable manner.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Public education and effective communication on the intent and purpose of this Bill after its Third Reading will be useful.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I hope the Minister for Law will spare no effort to dispel the misconstrued idea that curtailment on freedom of speech and on expression of disagreement against the Government is the purpose of this Bill; and this should be done in the social media also.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Although the educational level in Singapore is very high, we cannot assume that what is debated and discussed is readily understood and noticed by the general public.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: There is also a need to better inform with good and clear communications on the punishments for contempt in matrimonial disputes as doing so may serve as a preventive measure for potential defaulters.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Thus, public education in this area will have to be targeted with a simple, easily understood and multilingual message brought to the ground where it matters.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Hopefully, success in effective communications will reduce the number of possible contempt of Court cases in matrimonial disputes.

sections.label: Bill defines contempt conduct types
sections.summary: Part 2 of the Bill lays out contempt conduct: sub judice publication, scandalising the Court, and disobeying Court orders or undertakings.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: For the layman, the Bill clearly lays out in Part 2 the types of conduct that amount to contempt; the key ones being: one, sub judice or publishing content that may interfere with or prejudice an ongoing Court case; two, scandalising the Court through acts that impute improper motives or attack the integrity or impartiality of the Court; the strength of the Judiciary being founded in the confidence and respect of the people in the justice system; and three, intentionally disobeying a Court order or breaching an undertaking to the Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: As someone keenly interested in social service matters, I am particularly glad that the Bill makes it clear on the consequences of defying Court orders when obligations of maintenance payments are not fulfilled.

sections.label: Defences and punishment ceiling
sections.summary: Editors are not liable without authority, content or knowledge, and honest reasonable failure to obey Court orders is a strong defence, with a punishment ceiling now in place.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Persons exercising editorial duties are not liable for publishing or distributing contemptuous content, if the latter was done without their authority, content or knowledge.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: And one that I fully applaud is that provided in clause 21, where there is honest and reasonable failure to obey a Court order, as in the case of persons who might be illiterate or genuinely unaware of his or her obligations, the Court will consider this to be a strong defence and not rule the act as contempt.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I appreciate the fact that where there is currently no limit on the punishment which may be imposed for contempt of Court, a ceiling is now put in place for punishment.

sections.label: Support for sub judice definition
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill defining sub judice as a primary act of contempt, upholding fair trial and presumption of innocence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Regardless of our personal sentiments on those charged and the nature of their charges, the principle of according each defendant the right to remain innocent until proven guilty and a fair trial must be upheld.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I am thus supportive of the Bill in defining sub judice as one of the primary acts of contempt of Court.

sections.label: Petition concerns about the Bill
sections.summary: The speaker says the Petition's concerns about the Bill stifling discourse will be considered through three aspects of the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Those who strike at it, strike at the very foundation of society." And that is why, when the Petition is brought, which suggest that this Bill stifles active and public discourse, we should sit up and look at it, because these are, indeed, very serious suggestions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, let me consider these concerns, outlined in the Petition, in the context of three aspects of the Bill: first, whether the Bill aims to stifle active and responsible discussion; second, the power given to the AG to issue a non-publication direction; and third, the proposed punishments which have been seen or described in the Petition as being out of step with benchmarks.

sections.label: Contempt: scandalising and sub judice
sections.summary: A person is liable for contempt for statements scandalising the Court, undermining public confidence in justice, or making sub judice statements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Second, a person will be liable for contempt for statements which scandalise the Court, or which undermines public confidence in the administration of justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: And third, a person will be liable for contempt for sub judice statements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: This means where a person makes a statement which may interfere with or affect a fair trial or which amounts to public prejudgment of a case.

sections.label: Test in clause 3(1)(b)
sections.summary: Clause 3(1)(b) has two conjunctive limbs: an act risking prejudice to legal proceedings and a publication tending to prejudice a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The test is found in clause 3(1)(b) of the Bill and has been frequently discussed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: There are two limbs to it: first, it has to be an act which risks prejudicing legal proceedings and – this is conjunctive – a publication which tends to prejudice a fair trial of a case.

sections.label: AG non-publication direction power
sections.summary: The clause lets the AG direct a publisher to stop publishing if satisfied it is in the public interest and with High Court leave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The clause allows the AG to direct a publisher of any matter to refrain from or cease publishing that matter, if he is satisfied that it is in the public interest to do so, and if he has the leave of the High Court.

sections.label: Bill clarifies process, adds safeguards
sections.summary: The Bill makes the process clearer and introduces express safeguards by prescribing the legal test the AG must satisfy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: The Bill simply makes the process clearer and introduces express safeguards by prescribing the legal test which the AG must satisfy when he goes to Court to seek a non-publication order.

sections.label: Balance and AG's clause 13 power
sections.summary: Clause 13 gives the AG this power to strike a balance, but it is not unfettered and requires the leave of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: But this is not a case of absolutes, it is a case about striking the right balance, having regard to how quickly a publication can go viral, and it is in this context alone that clause 13 gives the power to the AG in the form that it does.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It also bears noting that this power is not unfettered, and the AG will require the leave of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: And in order to get such leave, it will need to satisfy the Court that the acts, in fact, constitute prima facie contempt, and the Court will be guided by the principles set out in this very same Bill, before the order would be granted.

sections.label: Contempt punishment upper limits
sections.summary: The Bill sets maximum contempt punishments for the High Court and Court of Appeal: a $100,000 fine, three years' imprisonment, or both.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: While the State Courts Act prescribes an upper limit for the District and Magistrates Courts, the Supreme Court of Judicature Act does not currently prescribe an upper limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, this Bill directly addresses this ambiguity by setting out the maximum punishment that can be meted for the offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Clause 12 of the Bill thus states that where the power to punish for contempt is exercised by the High Court or the Court of Appeal, then a person who commits such contempt shall be liable to a fine not exceeding $100,000 or with punishment not exceeding three years, or both.

sections.label: Contempt punishment examples
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal recently punished a contemnor with eight months' imprisonment, while UK punishments recently ranged from eight to 21 months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In some cases, as our Court of Appeal recently did, a contemnor was punished with eight months' imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In the UK, recently, the punishment ranges from eight to 21 months.

sections.label: Contempt punishment across all types
sections.summary: The power of punishment applies across all types of contempt, including breach of protection orders for harassment, family violence, asset division and child maintenance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Notably, and I would like to emphasise too, that the power of punishment applies across the board to all types of contempt, including cases of breach of protection orders for harassment, family violence, as Members have heard from our colleagues earlier, those which relate to the division of assets and for maintenance in the care of children.

sections.label: Court of Appeal disagreed with punishment
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal expressly disagreed with the punishment offered, calling it an entirely undeserved discount that should not be taken as precedent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: But what my colleagues may have omitted to take note of is the fact that the Court of Appeal, in that case, actually expressly disagreed with the punishment that was offered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: It, in fact, said that this was an entirely "undeserved discount" and which will and should not be taken as a precedent.

sections.label: WP opposes Administration of Justice Bill
sections.summary: The WP states that it opposes the Administration of Justice (Protection) Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   ﻿Mdm Speaker, firstly, the WP wants to clearly state that we oppose this Administration of Justice (Protection) Bill.

sections.label: Publication definition covers private discussions
sections.summary: Under the Bill's definition of publication, private discussions via Facebook, verbal words or SMS, and coffee shop small talk, could be construed as contempt of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: According to the definition of "publication" under the Bill, even private discussions, where a view is communicated from one person to another, whether it is through Facebook among friends, verbal words or short message service (SMS), could be construed as contempt of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Ordinary citizens engaging in small talk at coffee shops could possibly be seen as contempt of Court and charged by the Government.

sections.label: Ministers and contempt of Court
sections.summary: A 1967 High Court judgment held that a Minister's statement can constitute contempt and that the Court judges whether it interferes with justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What he said was: "It does not follow that a statement made or issued by a Government Minister can never constitute contempt of Court, or that a Government Minister should never be punished for contempt of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A Minister of the Government is not above the law." The important principle behind this High Court judgment in 1967 is that the Court will judge whether a Minister's statement interferes with the administration of justice or not.

sections.label: Timeline of contempt Bill
sections.summary: The Bill was first raised by former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong in 2010, with later statements in 2012 and 2013, and one change from real risk to risk.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And what has been the timeline for this Bill?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This was first raised by former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong in 2010 in his Opening of Legal Year speech where he said that he had asked me to consider enacting such a law.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In May 2012, I stated that MinLaw intends to put the law of contempt in statutory form and was working on a draft Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Former AG Steven Chong said in Opening of the Legal Year 2013 that the Ministry was working with AGC on the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And I suspect I will be making this point numerous times.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is only one change in terms of scandalising the Court from "real risk", it has come down to "risk".

sections.label: Contempt law after Bill
sections.summary: If passed, the Act will be the same as current law on heads of contempt, except the test in scandalising the Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The law tomorrow, if the Bill is passed into an Act, will be exactly the same as the law today in terms of the heads of contempt, except for the test in scandalising the Court.

sections.label: Government statements and Court arbiters
sections.summary: Government statements are drafted with AG advice to avoid prejudicing proceedings, and Courts are the final arbiters.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Government's statements are carefully drafted with advice from the AG to try and not prejudice ongoing proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In Lau Swee Soong's case, the statements were a little bit more direct than the usual Government statements.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But I confirm for the record that Courts are the final arbiters.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They have to be the final arbiters if the rule of law has got any meaning.

sections.label: Contempt law largely unchanged
sections.summary: The law on contempt tomorrow will be pretty much the same as it is today.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The law tomorrow is going to be pretty much the same as it is today on contempt.

sections.label: Explaining the one change
sections.summary: The speaker has explained in detail why one change is being made, while acknowledging the view that Courts' words should be followed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: People can take that point of view that we should stick to what the Courts have said.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And I have explained in some considerable detail why I am making that one change, and that is this.

sections.label: No backsliding to UK case
sections.summary: The speaker confirms there is no going back to the UK case and that real or actual prejudice must be shown.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think Assoc Prof Mahdev Mohan also asked me to confirm.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is no backsliding as it were; no going back to the UK case.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You got to show real risk of prejudice or actual prejudice.

sections.label: Courts as sole arbiter
sections.summary: The speaker says he has clarified that under the Bill the Courts are the sole arbiter.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Dennis Tan made the point that the Courts should be the sole arbiter.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think the assumption is that under the Bill, the Courts are not, and I have clarified the Courts are the sole arbiter.

sections.label: AG charge or middle way
sections.summary: The AG either charges him or lets him go, but the Bill creates a middle way where the AG need not charge.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The AG either charges him or lets him go.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But if this Bill is passed into Act, there is a middle way in that the AG does not necessarily have to charge.

sections.label: Additional avenue to lessen charges
sections.summary: The speaker says an additional avenue is being given to lessen the possibility of people being charged.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But it may also be possible he may choose that, once it is taken down, he feels that there is not further risk, and he can take a view.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We are giving an additional avenue to lessen the possibility of people being charged.

sections.label: Law after Bill passed
sections.summary: The speaker states the law from March when Benjamin Lim was discussed will remain the law after the Bill is passed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Whatever was the law in March when we discussed Benjamin Lim will be the law tomorrow after this Bill is passed, if it is passed.

sections.label: Advice from AGC on contempt
sections.summary: The speaker says he took advice from the AGC and distinguishes contempt from what is appropriate to be said.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I took advice from AGC and I did it.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is contempt and then there is what is appropriate and not appropriate to be said.

sections.label: Waiting for Coroner's inquiry
sections.summary: The speaker says matters should wait for the Coroner's inquiry, where facts are presented, evidence tested and findings made, and the law does not change.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It should wait for the Coroner's inquiry, all the facts are presented, within a certain legal framework, irrelevant stuff is excluded, the evidence is tested, findings are made and then we all discuss the facts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But having said that, my views on what is appropriate or not appropriate, I have set out, but the key point is, the law does not change.

sections.label: Justice Choor Singh on Government duty
sections.summary: Justice Choor Singh said it is the Government's duty to maintain law and order and give the public proper information about such a disturbance.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Justice Choor Singh said, "In my judgment, it is plainly the duty of the Government not only to maintain law and order but also to give the public as much information as it is proper concerning any such disturbance." Can anyone argue with that? "I find that the first respondent in authorising the issue of this statement by his Ministry was merely carrying out this duty." So, Mr Low Thia Khiang thinks that Justice Choor Singh is right, Ms Sylvia Lim thinks that Justice Choor Singh is right, a few others I think cited it.

sections.label: Discussion and fair trial
sections.summary: Discussion is proscribed only if it will prejudice a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Discussion is proscribed only if it will prejudice a fair trial.

sections.label: Clause 3(1)(b) not disjunctive
sections.summary: The speaker says clause 3(1)(b) is not disjunctive but is read together, and that this is clear.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about clause 3(1)(b) and I think I have said it is not disjunctive, it is read together, and I think that is quite clear.

sections.label: Witnesses not pressured
sections.summary: Witnesses are not pressured because the law is already in place.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Witnesses are not pressured because we already have the law in place.

sections.label: POHA harassment suits
sections.summary: As for POHA, the Government never sued for harassment.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As for POHA, the Government never sued for harassment.

sections.label: Undermining confidence in Judiciary
sections.summary: Showing a risk of undermining confidence in the Judiciary is the bright line.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Plus if you show a risk of undermining confidence in the Judiciary – that is your bright line.

sections.label: AG on Government statement action
sections.summary: If the AG thinks the Government's statement is not appropriate, action will lie.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If the AG thinks that the Government's statement is not appropriate, yes, action will lie.

sections.label: Facebook post and prejudicing proceedings
sections.summary: A Facebook post cannot pose a real risk of prejudicing proceedings unless the poster is the Prime Minister with a million followers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng asked about putting up a Facebook post.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I do not want to be standing here and giving legal advice, but I cannot see how putting up a Facebook post poses a real risk of prejudicing proceedings unless you are the Prime Minister with a million followers and everybody reads what you say.

sections.label: Police investigate contempt offence
sections.summary: Contempt has always been investigated by the Police with leave of the AG, and the Police can investigate an offence put into statute.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Contempt has always been an offence, contempt has always been investigated by the Police with leave of the AG.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Now that we are putting it into statute, who else but the Police can investigate an offence?

sections.label: Law Society President not charged
sections.summary: The Law Society President was not charged for contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Law Society President was not charged for contempt.

sections.label: Statements not in contempt
sections.summary: Many statements are not in contempt because they do not pose a real risk.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In reality, many statements are not in contempt because they do not pose a real risk.

sections.label: Contempt enforcement against recalcitrant spouses
sections.summary: Contempt proceedings may not always be the most appropriate way to enforce orders, being most effective against recalcitrant spouses able but unwilling to pay.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Contempt proceedings may not always be the most appropriate way to enforce these orders; most effective against spouses who are recalcitrant, able to pay but unwilling to pay.

sections.label: Inability to pay and contempt
sections.summary: A spouse who disobeys a maintenance order due to inability to pay commits contempt; motive is irrelevant to liability but may affect punishment.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Strictly speaking, a spouse who disobeys a maintenance order because he or she is unable to pay, commits contempt under the Bill and under the current law.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The spouse's motive in breaching the order is irrelevant to the issue of liability, but it may be considered in determining what the appropriate punishment is.

sections.label: Review of civil order enforcement
sections.summary: The Ministry is conducting a comprehensive review of the regime for enforcing civil Court orders, with the Civil Justice Review Committee examining the issue.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On a broader level, my Ministry is conducting a comprehensive review of the regime for enforcing civil Court orders in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I have asked the Civil Justice Review Committee, led by Senior Minister of State Ms Indranee Rajah, to look at this issue amongst other issues, and more details will be announced in due course.

sections.label: Companies' liability for user material
sections.summary: Companies will not be liable for material published by readers or users if they had no editorial responsibility or control, or took due care.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The companies will not be liable for such material published by their readers or users if they had no editorial responsibility or control over the material; or even if they had editorial responsibility or control, if they had taken due care to prevent the publication of such material.

sections.label: Consistency of permitted speech
sections.summary: Whatever you are allowed to say today, you are allowed to say tomorrow.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Basic point: whatever you are allowed to say today, you are allowed to say tomorrow.

sections.label: Bill and discussion of law
sections.summary: The Bill does not prevent the public or civil society from discussing or advocating change of the law, but requires keeping away from prejudicing proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill does not intend to, does not prevent the public or civil society from discussing or advocating change of the law, but just keep away from prejudicing or real risk of prejudicing the proceedings.

sections.label: Complaints about judge's conduct
sections.summary: Genuine complaints about a judge's conduct can be made to the Chief Justice and the CPIB, and proper investigations can be conducted.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Genuine complaints regarding a judge's conduct can be made to the Chief Justice and, as I said, to the CPIB, and proper investigations can be conducted.

sections.label: Contempt definition under Bill
sections.summary: What constitutes contempt has not changed materially under the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As I have said, what constitutes contempt has not changed materially under the Bill.

sections.label: AG and contempt decisions
sections.summary: The AG cannot decide contempt alone; he must persuade the High Court, which decides if challenged.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Kok Heng Leun expressed a concern that a publication will be in contempt as long as the AG deems them to be so at first sight.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is not for the AG to decide on his own.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He needs to go and persuade the High Court, prima facie at first, and then, if there is a challenge, the Court has got to look at it and decide.

sections.label: Industrial Arbitration Courts contempt provisions
sections.summary: The Industrial Relations Act sets out comprehensive provisions for dealing with contempt of the Industrial Arbitration Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Industrial Relations Act has set out comprehensive provisions for dealing with contempt of the Industrial Arbitration Courts.

sections.label: Tribunal orders under Bill
sections.summary: Small Claims Tribunal orders are enforceable as Magistrate's Court orders, and Employment Claims Tribunal orders as District Court orders, so both are subject to this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Orders by the Small Claims Tribunal are enforceable as orders of a Magistrate's Court and will, therefore, be subject to this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Orders of the Employment Claims Tribunal will be enforceable as an order of a District Court and, therefore, subject to this Bill.

sections.label: AG leave and Police powers
sections.summary: Clause 13(7) says the High Court must grant the AG leave for a non-publication order, and clauses 22 to 24 enable Police arrests for contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: Clause 13(7) of the Bill says that once the AG shows the case satisfies certain conditions, the High Court "must" grant leave to the AG to issue a non-publication order. "Must".

sentences.speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
sentences.text: And clauses 22 to 24 enable the Police to arrest persons accused of contempt of Court, so there are additional Police powers in this field.

sections.label: Contempt requires prejudice or risk
sections.summary: Clause 3 requires showing prejudice or a real risk of prejudicing proceedings, not just casual talk.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Clause 3 says for the kind of contempt you are talking about, people sit with each other and sit in a coffee shop and say, "That fellow is guilty", and they say that over a beer.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But clause 3(1)(b) says you also got to show real risk of prejudicing the proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It shows that you must either prejudice or show a real risk of prejudice.

sections.label: Courts as ultimate arbiters
sections.summary: The speaker put on record that Courts are the ultimate arbiters of whether Executive power was exercised per the clause.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I did not have to disclose it but I put it on record.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I said that the Courts are the ultimate arbiters as to whether the power of the Executive was exercised in accordance with the clause.

sections.label: Government belief subjective test
sections.summary: The question asks whether the clause's 'Government believes it is necessary' wording makes the test subjective and narrows Courts' review power.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The Minister keeps saying that the Court is still the final arbiter of whether the Government has exercised its powers within the clause.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: But really, when you look at the phrasing of the clause, the operative words are "the Government believes it is necessary".

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Would the Minister agree with me that that introduces a subjective element to the test, that it is the Government's opinion that counts and the Court cannot substitute its own opinion as to whether it is necessary?

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: And we all know that this is very difficult to prove.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: So, I would like the Minister to confirm that this is actually a significant scoping down of the Courts' power to review the Government's assessment of what is necessary.

sections.label: Police power to investigate contempt
sections.summary: The question seeks clarification on which law lets Police investigate AG contempt complaints and whether contempt is arrestable under the CPC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: For example, in the Thaipusam matter in 2015, where he actually referred to the three accused and said that they did various things before the Court came to a conclusion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The Minister said that the Police have always had the power to investigate contempt on a complaint of the AG.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I would like his clarification on which law he is referring to say that the Police can be mobilised to investigate complaints by the AG of contempt of Court and is there actually any current law which states that contempt is to be treated as an arrestable case under the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) because I have not seen this myself?

sections.label: Government statement not contempt
sections.summary: A statement made on behalf of the Government is not contempt if the Government believes it necessary in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A statement made by a person on behalf of the Government is not contempt if the Government believes that such a statement is necessary in the public interest.

sections.label: Court rules on Government belief
sections.summary: The Court rules whether the Government's belief is accurate or the statement had a different motive intended to prejudice proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As with any other governmental power, ultimately, that is also a subject for the Court to rule on as to whether the Government's belief, Government's statement that it believes is accurate or whether the statement, in fact, had a different motive and a different reason and was intended to prejudice the proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If we come within the rubric of what Justice Choor Singh had said, that if you make a statement calculated to prejudice on-going proceedings, that will take the Government out of clause 3(4).

sections.label: Bill not saving past contempt
sections.summary: The Bill will not save anyone who already committed contempt, and the law takes effect tomorrow if passed today.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If I had committed contempt, this Bill is not going to save me because the contempt has already been committed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This law takes effect from tomorrow if we pass it today.

sections.label: Law not retrospective
sections.summary: The law cannot relate to anything that happened before tomorrow.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: First of all, this law cannot relate to anything that happened before tomorrow.

sections.label: Population support and no impact
sections.summary: A vast majority supports the Bill, with 249 signatories, and the Bill has no substantive impact on the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A vast majority of the population supports the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think you know the number of people who signed it − 249, as far as I can tell.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And even if people think that something is not correct, then we have the duty to go out and persuade and explain.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: This Bill has, first of all, as I have been pointing out at various times, no substantive impact on the law.

sections.label: Harm to AG's case
sections.summary: The question is more about speed, because things can travel at lightning speed all over.

sentences.speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
sentences.text: What harm would it do to the AG's case if it was a justifiable case to start with?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is more the question of speed, Mr Tan, because, nowadays, when something is put up, it can travel at lightning speed all over.

sections.label: AG quick court order
sections.summary: The balance is giving the AG a quick right to go to Court and get an order if he satisfies the Court prima facie.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You balance that by first giving the AG a quick right to go to Court and get an order if he can satisfy the Court, prima facie.

sections.label: Courts as ultimate arbiters
sections.summary: The Courts are the ultimate arbiters of statutory interpretation and whether the Government's exercise of powers comes within that provision.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Courts are the ultimate arbiters of a statutory interpretation and whether the Government's exercise of the powers come within that provision.

sections.label: Contempt penalty chilling effect
sections.summary: A Member asks whether the new maximum penalty of $100,000 and three years could chill free speech by Singaporeans of limited means.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Would the Minister not acknowledge that one difference between the law yesterday and what the law will be tomorrow is that tomorrow, on the statute books, there will be a maximum penalty of $100,000 and three years, a penalty that is very far away from past sentencing precedents for contempt of Court cases?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Does the Minister not acknowledge that that could well have a chilling effect on Singaporeans of limited means exercising the right to free speech getting involved in debates and discussions on matters of public interest if there is even a slightest remotest risk of prosecution under this law?

sections.label: Penalty now limited
sections.summary: The Minister replies that the penalty was previously unlimited but will be limited once the Bill comes into force.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The difference is that previously, it was unlimited.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Today, if the Bill is passed, once it comes into force, it will be limited.

sections.label: Voting results and amendment withdrawal
sections.summary: The vote is declared 72 Ayes, 9 Noes, no Abstentions, and amendments to clauses 3 and 13 are withdrawn.

sentences.speaker: Mdm Speaker
sentences.text: I will now proceed to declare the voting results.

sentences.speaker: Mdm Speaker
sentences.text: There are 72 "Ayes", 9 "Noes", and no "Abstentions".    .

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
sentences.text: On behalf of Mr Kok Heng Leun and Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, we would like to withdraw our amendments, both for clauses 3 and 13 together.

sentences.speaker: The Chairman
sentences.text: I reconfirm that you are withdrawing the amendments to clauses 3 and 13?

sentences.speaker: The Chairman
sentences.text: That being the case, I shall take all the remaining clauses together.

sections.label: Third reading vote
sections.summary: On the question that the Bill be read a Third time, there are 72 Ayes, 9 Noes and no Abstentions.

sentences.speaker: Mdm Speaker
sentences.text: The question is, "That the Bill be read a Third time." There are 72 "Ayes", 9 "Noes", and no "Abstentions".
